newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FOCUS-Czech inflation hits low but no rate cut seen.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Czech inflation hits low but no rate cut seen.

text.p: Czech consumer inflation continued its downtrend, hitting an all-time low in March, but analysts said upcoming price increases from government deregulation should take away any room the central bank has to lower interest rates.
Month-on-month the consumer price index (CPI) eased to 0.1 percent from 0.3 percent in February.

That put the year-on-year figure at 6.8 percent, the lowest since the Czech Republic became independent at the start of 1993 and down from 7.3 percent the previous month, the Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) said on Tuesday.
The key sliding average inflation figure, which uses 1993 as a base, edged down to 8.4 percent from 8.6 percent in February, and was down from nine percent in March 1996.
The inflation data were below market expectations, with a Reuters survey of economists on Monday predicting a 0.4 percent monthly increase.

"The figures are a little lower than expected but I don't think that this will change opinions on the development of inflation over the coming months," said Pavel Sobisek, an analyst at Zivnostenska Banka.
The CSU said in a statement that the main factors keeping the March figure low were a 0.1 percent drop in the price of foodstuffs, drinks and tobacco, and in the leisure sector.
Price deregulation influenced the seasonally-adjusted rate by 0.014 percent, while seasonally-adjusted core inflation was 0.287 percent.

But analysts said a rate cut by the Czech Central Bank (CNB) was unlikely because price deregulation and planned increases to post and telephone rates in April were expected to cause a jump in inflation by some two percentage points.
"The numbers are good...but in general terms I don't think there is still any space for a loosening of the central bank's tight monetary policy," said Martin Kupka of Patria Finance.
In March the government approved proposals to raise household electricity prices by 15 percent and rents at state-controlled housing by an average of 50 percent, effective July 1.
Many Czechs still live in flats with artificially low rents and with energy bills subsidised by industrial users.

Last summer the CNB raised its key discount rate one percentage point to 10.5 percent, and hiked minimum reserve requirements to 11.5 percent from 8.5 percent of deposits to squeeze off surging domestic demand.
Analysts said the moves served to restrict growth of the money supply significantly and ease inflationary pressures.
Growth in the money supply stood at 7.8 percent at the end of December, well below the central bank's 13 to 17 percent growth target for 1996, and in the middle of its 8-12 percent range for 1997.
But central bank officials have warned that wage growth -- which was up 16.2 percent in nominal terms in February -- and its influence on inflation is a growing concern.
Central bank officials were not immediately available for comment on the inflation figures.
Despite the favourable CPI data, the Czech crown lost ground as some market players pushed the currency lower .
In morning trading, the crown was at 29.420 against the dollar and 17.163 to the mark, implying a 1.80 percent rise against the basket midpoint, down from an opening at 2.20 percent.
At midday, the central bank followed the trend with its daily fixing, putting the crown/dollar at 29.430 and crown/mark at 17.161, or 1.80 up against the basket.

"The first thought for players was that the lower figures increase the fear of a rate cut," said Petr Korous of bank CSOB. "But the market is more or less balanced between those who play that first idea against those with a contrary view."
